speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO MAINTAIN ESSENTIAL SERVICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the President of the Treasury Board. I understand that the talks have resumed with the GTL union, and that is encouraging, but I would like to ask the minister, in view of the fact that the services designated as essential to the safety and security of the public are not being maintained, in violation of the law, what he is doing to avoid a tragedy that might occur any day as the result of services designated as essential to the safety and security of the public being illegally withdrawn?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (President of Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO MAINTAIN ESSENTIAL SERVICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when public servants holding positions designated as essential do not report to work and are on strike, they are violating the law. We are collecting data to submit as evidence and we have decided to prosecute in each case. Evidently, the directors of the programs involved will take the necessary steps to maintain security and if there is no staff, they will take the necessary decisions to protect the public.

subsubtopic: STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO MAINTAIN ESSENTIAL SERVICES
speechtext: May I ask the President of the Treasury Board whether his assertions about taking measures to examine cases in which these services are withdrawn is not in fact all talk, and that he is doing nothing effective to ensure that essential services are maintained? Granted that this parliament has given the right to strike, is it not equally the law of this land that services designated as essential to the safety and security of the public be maintained, and has the minister any measure to put forward in this regard which is not totally ineffective?

subsubtopic: STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO MAINTAIN ESSENTIAL SERVICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we cannot compel public servants to come back to work. The departments concerned will take the necessary steps to assure public security. All departments have let us know that they have occasionally suspended some services because they did not have full staff. As for us, we are taking all legal proceedings at our disposal to penalize the individuals who have been violating the law. As I said, in no circumstance will we withdraw the proceedings lodged before the courts, because we feel that all civil servants must obey the law.

subtopic: STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP-REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT ACTION TO SETTLE

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP-REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT ACTION TO SETTLE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Acting Prime Minister. With the grain shipments in the country being blocked, the postal service in virtual chaos and the law of this parliament sponsored by this government being broken with impunity to the danger of the public, will the Acting Prime Minister as head of this government do more than simply reaffirm the faith of the government in collective bargaining will he start governing this country, or is he prepared to sit back and watch the country drift into chaos?

subtopic: STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP-REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT ACTION TO SETTLE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP-REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT ACTION TO SETTLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague the President of the Treasury Board has given every assurance that the law of this country will be enforced. It is the law of this country that people do have the right to strike. It is the law of the country that certain designated employees who are essential to public safety and security should work. My colleague the President of the Treasury Board is saying that he is accumulating evidence. There are procedures provided in the law for dealing with such cases. He is follow-
Oral Questions
ing those procedures, and I do not think that he can go any further than to enforce the law itself. It may be that this parliament will want to reverse itself and deprive strikers of the right to strike, but that is a decision for which we would have to take responsibility if the time comes for that action. In the meantime, I believe that we should support the law as it now stands.

subtopic: STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP-APPLICATION TO STAFF RELATIONS BOARD FOR CONSENT TO PROSECUTE THOSE WHO STRIKE ILLEGALLY
STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP-APPLICATION TO STAFF RELATIONS BOARD FOR CONSENT TO PROSECUTE THOSE WHO STRIKE ILLEGALLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will direct my first supplementary to the President of the Treasury Board and ask him if, in connection with the investigation and the accumulation of evidence with respect to illegal activity in the present difficulty, he has as yet made an application to the Staff Relations Board for consent to prosecute where there is clear evidence of illegality.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (President of Treasury Board):
subtopic: STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP-APPLICATION TO STAFF RELATIONS BOARD FOR CONSENT TO PROSECUTE THOSE WHO STRIKE ILLEGALLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as soon as the evidence is provided to my ministry by the different departments, we will proceed to go before the board to get permission to prosecute under the law, as members of parliament have written it. I am very surprised that at one minute hon. members tell me that I am too tough and the minute after they tell me that I am not tough enough. Since the first day I have been consistent. Everyone who is acting illegally will be prosecuted, and there will be no withdrawal of any cases to buy peace. If it is the wish of this parliament to change the system and any hon. member is so bright, their ideas can be brought before the joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate studying the Finkelman Report.

subtopic: STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP-REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE NO INTERVENTION BY MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES IN LEGAL STRIKE
STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP-REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE NO INTERVENTION BY MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES IN LEGAL STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question is not whether this parliament has given certain rights with respect to the collective bargaining process. That is not the question in front of us at all. The minister should not try to dilute a very serious issue with his offhand, casual remarks.
My supplementary question is directed to the Minister of National Defence, and I hope that the President of the Treasury Board pays some attention to it because part of our difficulty arises out of this. Can the Minister of National Defence and his colleague assure us that they have taken steps to reinforce earlier instructions to base commanders at Canadian armed forces bases across Canada to prevent members of the Canadian armed forces from undertaking work activities normally carried out by employees who are legally out on strike. Shutdown of service is occurring not only with defence; I think all hon. members realize in other areas of public service total shutdown of service has come about.

essential services. In the case of illegal strike activity, the forces will only become involved in carrying on those essential services. They will not be involved in strikebreaking. They will not be involved in interfering in any case where the personnel concerned are legally on strike.

As for the other question, of course this government is not a strike-breaker and does not intend to be.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the hon. member's question, I should first clarify for him his reference to the waters in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. The government of Canada regards these waters as historic Canadian waters. As such, they are internal waters of Canada. The laws of Canada apply to them in the same way they apply to the waters of our inland lakes. That position has been reaffirmed over the years, going back to the early administrations. I believe in 1949 the Prime Minister of the day reiterated that Canadian government position in the House of Commons.
With respect to the second part of the hon. member's question, last week I made a fairly comprehensive statement in that historic city of Halifax on the whole question of law of the sea. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUATE TRANSPORTATION POLICY-REQUEST THAT FUNCTION OF DEPARTMENT BE REVIEWED BY HOUSE
speechtext:
That this House questions the ability of the Ministry of Transport on its past and present record to provide and to run a modern, safe, efficient and co-ordinated transportation system for Canada's national and regional economies, its foreign trade and its social needs-as promised Canadians in the Speech from the Throne; refers to that ministry's repeated failure to provide interim remedies for urgent transportation problems while Canada awaits that promised transportation system; and recommends that the structure, function and performance of that ministry be forthwith reviewed in depth by this House.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I should like to start this debate by saying that we on this side of the House look forward to debating the subject of transportation, certainly in its public form. We feel that transportation has suffered under the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) during the last few years. We hope in our contribution to outline some of the more salient points of the problems so far as transportation is concerned. We also hope the minister will engage in this discussion today and possibly set down some guidelines as to the direction transportation policy in this country will be taking. We feel it is very important and critical that this be spelled out in as clear terms as possible.
Frankly, we are skeptical when the minister says that he intends to introduce a transportation policy in the next few weeks or months. We will not believe it until we see it. I hope the minister will keep on saying this another fifty times until it happens. We believe transportation under this administration, especially under the present minister, has been allowed to deteriorate to a point where it now operates to the detriment certainly of regional development, particularly as applied to the two extremities of the country, the Atlantic region and the western provinces.

speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. It is indicative of the whole transportation system in this country that the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) would have to rise on a point of order. It would seem that the minister and the government do not care at the present time, and I say that sincerely. I was saying that Canada's transportation system so far as can be determined, is working to the detriment of regional development, particularly as it applies to the so-called extremities of the country, namely, the Atlantic region and the western provinces. Each sector of the current transportation system appears to have been developed in isolation from the other sectors. Consequently, there is no integration and the ability to enter into any long-range planning has been virtually nullified. We see the results of that at present.
Canadian travellers have been plagued by increasing costs and an increasingly poor quality of service, as anybody who has travelled across this country knows. I believe that in general the government is subsidizing substantially a transportation system that operates contrary to the public interest and which in many cases appears to be in a shambles. I suppose, that the words of the minister regarding the governments transportation policy will be quoted to him again and again. He said that it is in a mess. More recently the minister stated that transportation in Canada is in even more of a mess than anyone realizes. However, he has consistently refused to do anything about it. In fact, we often find the minister-this has happened in the last two or three weeks-either in the House of Commons, in committees or outside the House, in front of the public, actually making a laughing-stock of his department and of the Canadian transportation system. The election promises made in the 1974 campaign appear to have been lost in a maze of meaningless declarations of intent, and all we have left is a self-confessed mess.
The problem may be better illustrated by an examination of the haphazard framework within which each section of the transportation system is allowed to operate. As I mentioned before, they appear to be operating at times in complete isolation one from another. For example, air transportation at present exists in what must be termed a complete policy void. In November of 1973 the Minister of Transport announced route divisions between Air Canada and CP Air, claiming all the while that his statement was the first of three announcements which would complete the over-all review of air transportation policy. More than a year and a half has passed since he made that statement, with no further policy announcements coming from his department, despite the fact that in March of 1974 he informed us that the transportation system was in a state of chaos.
Air Canada, which will be discussed later in the debate, our national airline, recorded in 1973 a profit of about $12 million. In 1974, as everyone knows, it recorded a deficit in the neighbourhood of $9 million. Between 1973 and 1974, CP Air-which is Air Canada's chief competitor-registered a substantial profit. Admittedly, it was lower than the previous year's, but it was still a profit.
According to the minister's department and the public statements that we have heard, no one seems to know why

Air Canada is losing money, nor does its president, Mr. Yves Pratte. Mr. Pratte claims, through the press and in speeches he has made that, on one hand, the deficit was caused by tremendous competition from the air charter companies, when we know that the national airline is the largest charter operator in the country, and on the other hand he claims that these losses have been experienced because of increased subsidization of short-haul routes by longer routes. Yet the five regional air carriers which are confined to short-haul routes all recorded substantial profits in 1974.
My contention is that at present morale in Air Canada, especially among the employees who work with the travelling public, the ones whom you and I see when we go to an airport, is low. But I would point out that I do not believe that is necessarily the fault of the employees. Rather, it is the result of the complete lack of direction by top management personnel in Air Canada. I also contend that Air Canada is top-heavy so far as its management is concerned. This is unfortunate because it is what happens so often in government-owned corporations or agencies. It seems to be an almost built-in instinct of the people in the top echelons of these corporations to appear to create virtual empires for themselves, thus destroying the whole intent of a nationally-owned enterprise.
Another example of the contradiction that exists in our air policy-there have been other examples since-is in the application which was made back in 1973 for an air carrier to service Thunder Bay and Sudbury. Nordair, which is the regional airline operating out of Montreal, applied for permission to operate a service to Sudbury and Thunder Bay. After receiving assurances from the communities involved that Air Canada was not willing to service these areas-that was the basis of their application-an application was made to the Canadian Transport Commission in December of 1973.
Nordair had examined the route in accordance with the 1966 regional airline principles and came to the conclusion that it was within its legal boundaries when applying for the route allocation. Within two weeks of Nordair's application, Air Canada announced its intention to service the Thunder Bay-Sudbury area, having repeatedly refused to do so in the past. Nordair applied to the Canadian Transport Commission, which decided that under the terms of the Air Canada licensing contract established by the Air Canada Act, the national airline can connect any points within the boundaries of its licensing charter if it so wishes. Needless to say, Nordair has appealed this decision.
This is the kind of constraint under which third level air carriers operate, and this is where changes should be considered. Because such situations might arise in the future, the entire Air Canada Act should be reviewed. Spokesmen for the regional airlines contend that if the Air Canada contract states that that airline may pre-empt the application of any other airline, that will have a discouraging effect. I am inclined to agree with them and I think it will create an inhospitable climate for future investment and development.
We must realize that the airline industry depends on what is termed long lead time for planning future development. In the current, non-directional framework that

exists, the only airline capable of any sort of long-range planning-sometimes we wonder whether it does any meaningful long-range planning-is Air Canada itself. This is certainly to the detriment of other sectors of the industry which I contend can operate for the good of the Canadian public as well as Air Canada is supposed to, provided we can introduce the kind of competition that I believe is necessary to make Air Canada a more efficient airline.
Another area of grave concern to the Canadian public is the framework within which the railways operate in terms of policy guidelines. I contend, as I did at the outset of my speech, that we do not have at the present time any policy guidelines. An example of this is the whole question of railroad passenger service. If one considers this year's estimates which the Committee on Transport and Communications will be studying very shortly, he will see that approximately $200 million has been allocated to the subsidization of an uneconomic rail passenger line.
To give the House a little background, these payments are distributed to the railways for continued operation of passenger service in areas where the Canadian Transport Commission has decided that the continuation of service is essential to the interests of various regions. In other words, these payments ensure that through direct subsidization, in some cases an uneconomic rail passenger line will be continued. The system was devised in 1967 under the regulations of the National Transportation Act. In order to abandon a passenger line on which the railway is operating at a loss, the company must apply to the CTC before it can discontinue the service. Then the Canadian Transport Commission conducts a study into the effects the abandonment of the line would have on the region served. In approximately 98 per cent of the cases, the CTC has determined that discontinuation of the service would be to the detriment of the area concerned.
The end result of this process is the removal of any initiative by the railways to improve their services. They are always assured of receiving 80 per cent of what they lost in operating costs and I think it is natural, therefore, that they are neither inclined, nor are they forced, to better their services. The whole question of subsidies for uneconomic lines should be intensively investigated, especially in light of the current circumstances. By "current circumstances" I mean the present situation and also the advancements in technology which have occurred over the past few years. In the past few years the railways have been relegated to second place compared with air and automobile travel. Air transport has been singled out as the answer to our future travel requirements. However, with the uncertainties at the present time caused by the energy crisis and its potential effect on transportation, the railway in many countries, the United States in particular, have been resurrected and restored to a more favourable position.

The whole railway system for moving people must be intensively considered, especially in densely populated areas of the country. This question was discussed briefly the other day in the transport committee. In the densely populated areas of the country there is great need for a far better, high-speed rail service to move people around.
I hope the minister will also take regional air services into consideration for the more sparsely populated areas of Canada, such as the west. I think a legitimate question to consider is the aspect of allowing regional air services to play a far greater role in the movement of people in more sparsely populated areas such as Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
Mr. Speaker, grain movement affects a major part of our economy and also a major part of the land area in our country. It is a matter which will be dealt with more fully before our debate is over. In the area of grain movement there is virtually no policy direction by the government. There is virtually no policy to rationalize our grain handling system. A year ago we were talking about exporting a billion bushels of grain per year. At the present time, with the uncertainties in rail transportation and with tie-ups caused by the labour situation, exporting a billion bushels of grain per year is simply a pipe-dream.
The Minister of Transport cannot, and should not, take all the blame for the strike in Vancouver at the present time. He can take part of the blame because he is part of the cabinet which has refused to act in a positive way. He can, and should, take a good portion of the blame for the complete lack of policy guidelines defining what is needed in terms of grain movement in western Canada. We find that the self-appointed spokesman for western Canada, the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, has at times been making almost contradictory statements to those of the Minister of Transport.
The most glaring contradictions are in regard to the Crowsnest pass rates. The minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board has indicated that there will probably be a change in what is known as the Crow rate. The Minister of Transport stated the other day in committee that there will not be a change in the Crowsnest pass rate at least for the year 1975. The minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board has certainly attempted to overstep his own jurisdiction. He has muddied the waters as far as the discussion of transportation is concerned in western Canada, because no one really knows where the power lies in regard to any changes which may take place within the government.
In regard to suitable hopper cars to haul grain, there has been no policy decision whatsoever and the railways have stated flatly that they do not intend to purchase hopper cars to move grain. There has been almost complete indecision about rail line abandonment in western Canada, although there has been-giving the Department of Transport its dues-a decision to freeze any abandonment procedures on some 12,000 miles of track in western Canada until the year 2000. But as far as any policy in regard to rail line abandonment is concerned, there has not been a major policy decision.

Perhaps the Minister of Transport or his parliamentary secretary will outline this afternoon basically what the government intends to do as far as working toward a solution is concerned. I hope that his department has been in communication with the railways, the Wheat Board, the grain companies, the farmers and farm communities involved, because they all have to be taken into consideration when formulating an over-all rail policy for the movement of grain. The government has had the time to carry on this kind of negotiation. The Minister of Transport stated in committee that he would work toward a suitable grain handling system for western farmers, and we hope that today or in the very near future he will bring forward proposals in this regard.
In connection with strikes which pertain to grain shipments, the Canadian Wheat Board is going to cut off producer deliveries tonight because of lack of box car space. Unless the government sees fit to settle the present grain strike as soon as possible, certainly within the next few days, there may not be much of a grain industry left in western Canada to do very much about.
I am not going to take up the time of the House by talking about the effect of the strike on western Canada and, indeed, on the whole Canadian economy. I should like to say to the Minister of Transport, however, that when the strike is settled the government should seriously consider designating the movement of grain as an essential service so that workers in that industry will know exactly where they stand. The kind of situation that has arisen at the port of Vancouver is critical to the Canadian economy. In the past 11 years, the port of Vancouver has been shut down for 153 days because of strikes, and it will suffer irreparable harm if this situation is repeated. Another area of contention is the western economic opportunities conference as it pertains to freight rates, but I shall leave that subject for my colleagues who will be speaking later in the debate.
At present, the freight rate situation is in confusion, Mr. Speaker. The lifting of the freight rate freeze has heightened and accelerated the anomalies in the system and served to increase the kind of distress and to some extent the stagnation that has occurred in western Canada and the maritime region. The intended and publicly stated purpose of the freeze was to allow the federal government a time-frame within which an effective economic policy could be formulated. The freeze expired, however, void of any announcement whatsoever.
The disjointed policy development in this area is clearly illustrated in recent events concerning the various court decisions as to the legality of post-freeze increases. In these instances, as in others, lack of federal government direction and ministerial control has never been more evident. The decision taken by the Canadian Transport Commission accorded the railways approximately one-half of the 25 per cent increase they had applied for, and the rest on March 1, after a study period. The railways appealed to the Federal Court, which decreed that the CTC did not have the authority under the section of the act used to rule as they did. Consequently, the railways immediately began charging users the full increase.

As a result of this legal hassle, users of the system have had to operate under extremely confusing and unsettling conditions because from one day to the next freight was subject to different rates; there was no move by the minister or his department to set down any kind of direction.
The effects of greater efficiency in transportation services in Canada are far reaching. But in the absence of federal policy designed to promote and exploit this potential, the consequences for regional development and national unity could be, and are becoming, disastrous. In Canada, it can fairly be said that there is not only lack of transportation policy but lack of long-range planning toward the future development of such a policy. That is why we are skeptical of any policy announcement which may be coming out in the spring. This is a fact which may in future be responsible for the under-achievement of our national goals. In order to promote and encourage a successful economic future for Canada, a uniform strategy, formulated at the federal level and adopted by provincial, regional and municipal governments, is essential. Without the creation of such guidelines, Canadian development economically, regionally and socially will flounder.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say in all sincerity that we do not believe the Minister of Transport understands the importance of the role of transportation in Canadian life. I should qualify that by saying he either does not understand or does not care about the department. For that reason we are prepared to debate this resolution as strongly as we can because we feel it is important. We certainly hope that before the debate ends we can elicit a positive and meaningful response from the government in regard to guidelines and policy.

It is not impossible to have faster trains between Halifax, for example, St. John, and then on to Montreal and Toronto. Is it possible to have a better railway system along what is called the Quebec City-Windsor corridor? It is possible. It is a matter of determining the costs, knowing how to get the necessary equipment to the railways in due time, knowing how much steel is available, what manufactures are ready to operate. We are trying to establish a coherent system of transportation within the Maritimes. We cooperated with those provinces for the development of a subsidy policy acceptable to the companies and to the provinces. A 50 per cent subsidy is granted on all types of cargo going to Central Canada, both by rail and by truck. Maritime provinces are also getting an internal subsidy to help their development. Mr. Speaker, this morning I dealt with some of the achievements of the department which we are trying as much as possible to integrate into a comprehensive philosophy. I talked especially about the Maritimes. I only referred to a few of the ferries in the Maritimes, but there are other ferry services we looked after, for instance, as soom as a problem arose between Digby and St. John, I contracted the Canadian Pacific without delay to have the service restored.
When we had a problem between Yarmouth and Bar Harbour, I immediately got in touch with the province of Nova Scotia to solve that problem. We are trying to find a permanent solution so that under an agreement with a Swedish company, we can provide an efficient year-round service. In the Maritimes, we have the problem of a deep water harbour. There is also the problem of connecting Halifax and Montreal, the problem of Saint John, New Brunswick, the problem of ferries to Prince Edward Island, where a new shuttle service will soon start at Wood Island, and that is extremely important. It is a pity that the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) is not here, but we are going to build his control tower at Charlottetown, which means that Air Canada will have flights to Charlottetown. There will therefore be landing facilities in every Canadian province, including Prince Edward Island.
Of course, we have tried to solve every problem; it is a slow process. All those agreements are reached jointly with provinces, not just at Ottawa. We defend ourselves, we meet them, we have talks together, we try to settle problems. I had discussions with British Columbia and some other western provinces with respect to freight rates and the rates proclaimed under the bill which, by the way, has just been passed in Committee and should eventually be studied in this House. We settled the matter of railway rate grouping. We discussed the matter of ferries between Vancouver Island and the mainland.
There were discussions with Western Canada about the ports of Churchill, of Prince Rupert, of Vancouver, on the matter of the Western region carrier, Canadian Pacific Western Airlines. Now I have yet to hear the opposition put forward a policy on that matter; however, when a province takes hold of a carrier, it really is a serious matter... We are now formulating a comprehensive system, a third level of regional carriers.
This morning, I heard my friend, the hon. member for Lisgar, saying: Even regional carriers make money. Air Canada knows and says it. But do they know why? It is

precisely because they do not operate on a regional basis, they are mainly interested in chartered flights. They organise such flights to the Caribbean Islands, to Europe. It means that those companies, created to service small areas, have finally become companies with international interests and DC-8's and L10-ll's. Thus, they make money of course, because they have customers of a superior level. Then, of course, our national companies have to take travellers when it is not profitable. He forgot to tell us those things, probably because he did not know about them.
We tried to solve the problem of railway cars of which there was a shortage last year. They are used for carrying lumber, wheat and other commodities. We appointed a supervisor, and distribution has improved. Of course, when things are not moving, it is not the supervisor who is to be blamed, but the strike. Then, we discussed the maximum rates, for example, in the field of freight; we discussed road-beds tracks, overpasses. We discussed the Ashton-Clinton pass in British Columbia, which is so essential to speed up traffic to the ports. We discussed the national parks, crossing rates which have already been eliminated. There have been discussions about tracks relocation and legislation on that matter has already been passed. There have also been discussions about the doubling the tracks, so as to avoid, in some circumstances, passengers trains being delayed by freight trains.

Mr. Speaker, what is a transportation policy? We do not have all the answers. This is what we are trying to develop. That is why a great number of technicians are trying to find the best and most economical means of transportation for our freight.
For instance, in Canada, there is more and more emphasis on transportation from North to South with regard to the development of natural resources, whether it be the tar sands of Alberta, coal, sulphur, whether it be the natural resources of northern Ontario or even of Quebec. The attraction of the South is so strong that it is threatening the great line designed by Sir John A. Macdonald across Canada from East to West. It is a problem.
Now I shall put before you a very simple problem. We are presently extracting coal in Alberta and moving it to Ontario by railway. Now, it might be a better idea to produce electricity in Alberta and transmit it to Ontario. It is the best solution. Is someone in this House ready to give me an answer? A number of people have been working on this for several weeks and they have not found an answer yet. We do not know yet what is the most economical solution. We try to have a consistent and integrated transportation policy so that Canadians will have the best possible service.

Mr. Speaker, I am in no position to out-shout the minister. Loud shouting will not be sufficient to enunciate the policies of the government. I agree with the minister's statements concerning the official opposition in the context of their not saying what their policy is. I think he paid a backhanded compliment to the New Democratic Party in saying that we at least have advocated alternatives to what is being done by himself and his government.
I also want to caution the minister that every time the Minister of Transport receives criticism about the government's policies or lack of policies, he should not be so sensitive and attempt to construe this as some kind of racism. That has to be a strawman, a sign of desperation

and anger; but the minister must control his anger. He quoted two opposing views of the press and mentioned Mr. Fisher. I defy him to show us where at any time Mr. Fisher in his comments has been racist in respect of the minister or anyone else.
The minister should be prepared to take it, even if he does not like it. If he cannot stand the heat, he should get out of the kitchen, to quote Harry Truman. We in the New Democratic Party, for many years-certainly for the past three of four years-have been trying to persuade the minister, and I believe he has been persuaded to some extent, to accept our position. But he should recognize that his worst problem is within his own cabinet and the government. He has colleagues who insist on acting on nineteenth century concepts in respect of transportation. I am glad one Conservative applauded.

speechtext: One more than the NDP.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUATE TRANSPORTATION POLICY-REQUEST THAT FUNCTION OF DEPARTMENT BE REVIEWED BY HOUSE
speechtext:
This probably means at least one of them is not still in the nineteenth century. They pick on picayune questions. Their expertise tells them that anything which belongs to the people is bad. Air Canada-and the minister is right this time-compared to the CPR is terrible because the CPR shows a profit, and the CNR is terrible because the CPR shows a profit. Let me warn my friends to the right about the nineteenth century views which they have. The minister's colleagues have the same attitude. They have this glorious free enterprise concept. Transportation is a public utility which everyone must use. They continue to try to operate it in the way it was operated by the railroad barons of the 1890s. This is the type of attitude to which members of the Progressive Conservative Party and colleagues of the minister in his caucus still adhere.
Let me illustrate how good the CPR is in respect of public transportation and private enterprise. I know this may be difficult for free enterprisers to comprehend or accept, but the people of Canada have paid for all the profits of the CPR through subsidies in most years. In 1969 the CPR had a net operating profit of $31.4 million from its railway operations after fixed charges and income tax had been deducted. Their subsidies from the taxpayers of Canada that year amounted to $35 million. Had it not been for the subsidies by Canadian taxpayers in that year, the CPR would have had a loss of $3.6 million. In 1970 the CPR had profits amounting to $28.8 million, and received subsidies in the order of $30 million from the people of Canada. Without the subsidies, the CPR would have been $1.2 million in the hole in that year.

Of course on the railway and ancillary operations being trucks, hotels, telecommunications, ships and airlines. In 1971 the CPR showed operating profits, after fixed charges and income tax, of $38.6 million and received subsidies from the people of Canada of $40 million. We have been paying for this company even though we do not own it. We have been making sure there are dividends for the shareholders of $1.70 or $2.70. We have done this through subsidies.
Transportation

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUATE TRANSPORTATION POLICY-REQUEST THAT FUNCTION OF DEPARTMENT BE REVIEWED BY HOUSE
speechtext: Socialism for the rich.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUATE TRANSPORTATION POLICY-REQUEST THAT FUNCTION OF DEPARTMENT BE REVIEWED BY HOUSE
speechtext:
Private enterprise must have more profits even if it means using the taxpayers' money. The minister is justified in complaining about the official opposition, but what the official opposition, the New Democratic Party and the people of Canada want is his policy, not the Conservative policy or the NDP policy. We are not the government. What is the minister's policy? He wants the Conservative Party and the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board to tell him what he should do. If that is the position he is in, he should quit. If the minister is so bereft of some backbone, determination, imagination and political muscle in his own group that he must rely on the Progressive Conservative Party to tell him what their policies are so that he will know what to do, then he should quit.
The minister, who has worked very hard to solve these problems, has allowed events to occur over the past few years which have made the problems worse. I ask the minister how long he intends to sit back and allow one of his own colleagues to make statements, announcements and to start investigations, and so on, which have to do with transportation. This should be the minister's prerogative and responsibility. Who makes announcements and statements about branch lines? The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang). Who makes statements and announcements about the Crowsnest Pass rates? The Minister of Justice. Who makes announcements and sets up transportation committees under the Canada Grains Council? The Minister of Justice.
I ask, where the heck is the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand)? If I were Minister of Transport and one of my colleagues was doing that to me, I would say to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), "Look here; either he shuts up or here is my resignation". How long is the Minister of Transport going to sit back and take that nonsense? The Minister of Justice, if he gets his way, will be the architect of the further destruction and alienation of western Canada and of rural Canada in particular.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUATE TRANSPORTATION POLICY-REQUEST THAT FUNCTION OF DEPARTMENT BE REVIEWED BY HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUATE TRANSPORTATION POLICY-REQUEST THAT FUNCTION OF DEPARTMENT BE REVIEWED BY HOUSE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta), the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankow-ski), the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) and myself want to support the Minister of Transport on a transportation system that will allow us to live together as a country, that will preserve rural Canada and enable the grain producers to get their grain to the market.
The Minister of Justice announced what the government will do with the Crowsnest Pass rates. I will repeat, for the benefit of the Minister of Transport, what I said before the Minister of Justice, if it will help strengthen his position in the cabinet. The other night the minister said in the committee that the Crowsnest Pass rates are not like the Bible. I want to tell the Minister of Transport that he and his colleagues would have a better chance to amend the Ten Commandments that they would to amend the Crowsnest pass rates. Those rates are the one decent and fair deal our grain growers have had in our transportation

March 7, 1975
Transportation
system. Yet the Minister of Justice is trying to destroy that agreement. How much longer will the Minister of Transport stand for that nonsense?
With regard to the freight rates, I read again the communique put out at the Calgary meeting a week ago last Monday. The Minister of Transport said to his counterparts in the provinces that he will propose a legislative amendment to reduce rate differential anomalies between raw and finished products, and in the interim will consult the provinces and take measures necessary to correct urgent anomalies. He has consulted the provinces umpteen times since he became Minister of Transport and he knows what the anomalies are: they have been pointed out by the people of western Canada for the past 50 years.
If the Minister of Transport needs another couple of months to bring in his legislation, why does he sit back and allow the railroads to compound those inequities? It would only take two phone calls, one to the president of CNR and one to the president of CPR, telling them, "You will not increase any rate until we bring in this legislation". Instead of that, all the discrimination, the anomalies, the inequities and the absurdities in our freight rates structure are being compounded by increases in these rates.
To illustrate, let me refer to Burns and Company which are phasing out their meat packing plant in Prince Albert. Why are they doing it? Because the minister and his government sat back and allowed across the board rate increases that increased the spread between the cost of sending dressed beef and live cattle to central Canada. But the Minister of Justice supported the railways in the Supreme Court. The difference in cost between sending dressed beef and live cattle from Saskatoon to Montreal used to be 91 cents per 100 pounds. Now, as of March 1, it costs $1.17 more to ship dressed beef.
What does that do to our meat processing and packing industry in western Canada? It kills it. But the minister sits back and allows it to happen. All we have are the platitudes in his communiques telling us how he is going to correct these anomalies. He has been saying that ever since the day he became Minister of Transport-but he has yet to correct them. It is time he led, instead of waiting for the Conservatives, for members of the NDP and for the provinces to tell him what to do.
If I owned the Burns plant in Prince Albert, I would shut it down also. I would not want to own it either privately or publicly. Our freight rate and express rate structure make it economic suicide to try to operate a meat packing plant in Prince Albert, Saskatoon, or Regina. There is a perfectly logical reason for that. Any good management of a packing plant would close it down when the minister sits back and allows freight rates to be increased. A large part of the production of packing plants relies on the shipment of the product in small lots to hundreds of communities within several hundred miles of the location of the plant. What does the CNR do? Under our present transportation policy, the CNR cannot operate any differently from the CPR. It is told to be competitive and to make a profit: It is not told to provide service and to meet the transportation needs of Canadians no matter where they live.

What does the CNR do? Our own national railroad tells the retailers in Hudson Bay, Saskatchewan, and it tells Burns and Company in Prince Albert-only about 180 miles away-that they can ship, for example, 22 pieces of processed, packaged meat, or 610 pounds, which used to cost $21.80 or $3.57 a hundredweight, at a new rate of $33 or $5.40 a hundredweight. That is an increase of 52 per cent. Yet the minister allows these inequities to continue and to be compounded. I insist that all it takes is two phone calls, with the backing of the Prime Minister, of the government and of parliament, to the presidents of our two railways telling them that they are not to increase the rates at present. But the minister does not do it. Instead, he asks the Conservatives for their policy, as if that would be of any help. How desperate can you get for a policy if you have to ask the Conservatives? I am surprised that the minister is not a little more erudite than that.
I should like to make some comments about grain movement in the present situation. Everybody says that the workers have the right to strike. I give the minister full credit for standing by the right to strike, but he and the government have yet to make any significant move to remove the causes of strikes. Like the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), they say that the lowest paid public servants must show restraint. At the same time, they give an increase of $8,000 to $10,000 to deputy ministers and assistant deputy ministers. Increases are given to economists running around here who have Ph.Ds in the sex life of date palms. No restraint is required of them, they do not even have to bargain for increases: the cabinet and Treasury Board pass them through.
However, the lowest paid public servants are told they should show restraint. And the minister wonders why they shut down Vancouver harbour! He should have known that was the only result he would get. I want to propose something to the minister, something he has heard from me many times and with which he agrees, I am sure, in his heart and mind. He needs help and support in his own ranks. He must put a stop to the machinations and the dinosaur mentality of the Minister of Justice if he wants to succeed with a really national transportation policy in this country. As I said earlier, transportation is an essential public service; it is a public utility; it is something everybody has to use. Since that is the nature of transportation the minister must say in his new policy-which I hoped we would get today-that the major portion of the transportation system must be publicly owned and controlled. Consider any other country in the world, whether capitalist, communist, socialist or whatever: their transportation systems are publicly owned and publicly controlled. I spent a week in London the year before last; they know how to move people and goods.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUATE TRANSPORTATION POLICY-REQUEST THAT FUNCTION OF DEPARTMENT BE REVIEWED BY HOUSE

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUATE TRANSPORTATION POLICY-REQUEST THAT FUNCTION OF DEPARTMENT BE REVIEWED BY HOUSE
speechtext:
The first fundamental change the minister must bring about in transportation policy is the elimination of competition and profitability as the prime criterion for the operation of our railroads, airlines or other modes of transporation. The priority has to be service and making transportation systems available to meet the social and economic needs of our country, whether or not
March 7, 1975

they make money or lose money. It is as logical to have two competing railroads as it is to have two competing highway systems or two sewer or water systems.
If the minister would bear with me for a few more minutes, I will go into a little more detail. Given the principle of public ownership and control, given the principle of priority of service in meeting the transportation needs of this country and that competition and profitability take the lowest priority, it must follow that by integrating all modes of transportation each mode is assigned to its most sensible use. It is nonsense for trucks to be hauling loads from Toronto to Vancouver. It is uneconomic, it is inefficient and it flies in the face of everything all of us believe in regarding the consumption of energy and reducing pollution.
The minister proposes to put up about $157 million to improve the highway systems to take bigger load limits. That proposal flies in the face of all good sense about energy, pollution, safety and a decent, civilized community. It is equally nonsensical for a 100-car train to make short hauls of small lot shipments for 50 miles, 60 miles or 100 miles. That is the place for trucks. It is stupid for DC-9 and DC-8 jets to fly between Ottawa and Montreal: it is inefficient, wasteful of fuel and, again, flies in the face of all the things hon. members from all parties have talked about in this chamber for years.
Whether moved by bus, train or plane, our freight rates and passenger fares should be all-inclusive. Can the minister visualize somebody travelling from Ottawa, Ontario, to Peggy's Cove, Nova Scotia, buying one ticket with three coupons on it and going by train from Ottawa to Montreal, plane from Montreal to Halifax and bus from Halifax to Peggy's Cove, all of those modes being included in one fare? Each mode of transportation must be put to the best, the most efficient and the most sensible use.
Something must be done about the equalizing and/or subsidizing of fares and rates. We discriminate against people in our country because of where they happen to live. Will the minister face up to the fact of our geography, our climate and our people being scattered over 5,000 miles? It should be possible to fly from Toronto to Inuvik for the same price as from Toronto to Winnipeg. An equal-ized-subsidized system of freight rates would put an end to this mess in our freight rate structure. The minister needs to do something more than just talk about harbours, about $10 million in the estimates for three years in a row for the port at Churchill-and they are just now getting around to spending it. Again, the government has the imagination of a doorknob. For the port of Churchill $100 million is needed, not $10 million.

speechtext:
Thank you, Madam Speaker, and I thank my colleagues for their generosity and courtesy. I promise to be only five minutes and I think I can live up to that. I wish to continue with habours and terminals. Why do we need to put another one or two terminals in Vancouver? The place is so badly congested now that there is not enough room for a waiting ship to turn around. The shore space available for tracks and yards and warehouses is almost used up. What about another terminal in Prince Rupert? Even with the present facilities in Prince Rupert we could double the grain movement with one additional train per day for 42 weeks. For ten weeks of the year, when there are large snowfalls, rainfalls and slides, those trains do not run; but for 42 weeks an additional 11 million bushels could be moved into Prince Rupert and half a dozen of the ships in Vancouver could be loaded there. The same thing applies at Churchill. It can, and should be a six-month or seven-month a year port instead of three months. The allocated $10 million will not scratch the surface. Policy is needed in the area of integrated rail, air and bus transportation.
The dismal history of regional air carriers in this country is one of obtaining a franchise, sucking off a couple of lucrative routes from Air Canada and then telling us how they are going to serve a whole region. Then within a matter of months, or a year or two, they are begging for subsidies. All the time they are operating, the ability of Air Canada to provide service to people in the country, no matter where they live, is further decreased. If one were to add $1 to the fare of everyone who travels between Ottawa, Montreal, Toronto and Winnipeg, for example, one could fly from Toronto to Vancouver or Halifax for the same price. We would stop discriminating against people in this country because of where they happen to live.
Why do we need five or six airlines? It is inefficient and wasteful, with duplicate management. The regionals and the private carriers want the lucrative routes. They have forgotten that the purpose of transportation is to serve the needs of people. All they want to serve is their own interest, which is profit. This parliament and this government has to make up its mind about which comes first, people or profits.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUATE TRANSPORTATION POLICY-REQUEST THAT FUNCTION OF DEPARTMENT BE REVIEWED BY HOUSE

Tell that to Air Canada.

March 7, 1975
Transportation

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUATE TRANSPORTATION POLICY-REQUEST THAT FUNCTION OF DEPARTMENT BE REVIEWED BY HOUSE
speechtext:
The people of this country, if their transportation costs them money over and above the cost of passenger tickets and freight rates, will pay it. They do not expect their Post Office to make a profit, and never have. No post office that I know of in any country in the world has ever shown a profit. They do not expect their sewer, water and highway systems to show a profit. In 1967 we subsidized cars, trucks and buses to the tune of over $400 million. In the same year we subsidized the airlines, both public and private, to the tune of $170 million. In both cases that is more than the direct subsidies paid to the railroads.
Until the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) wins this battle in his own caucus and in cabinet he does not need to worry about what Conservative or New Democratic Party members say. Why does he keep asking conservatives for their policy? How desperate can you get? How bereft is the Liberal government? As soon as the minister makes a fundamental change in the direction and purpose of our transportation system then we will be able to move toward building a system that is integrated and efficient and, most of all, one that ensures that the social and transportation needs of the people of Canada will be met, no matter where they live.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUATE TRANSPORTATION POLICY-REQUEST THAT FUNCTION OF DEPARTMENT BE REVIEWED BY HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUATE TRANSPORTATION POLICY-REQUEST THAT FUNCTION OF DEPARTMENT BE REVIEWED BY HOUSE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am glad to have this opportunity to take part in the debate on the motion before us. I noticed on reading it that the wording was rather provocative, and I am not surprised that this debate took a stormy turn for a while. In any event, I did not have the pleasure to hear any of the speakers I heard, although there may have been good things said, raise the basic problem which is the cause of most of the difficulties we have to overcome in transportation.
First of all, what with the famous debt in each of those transportation areas? I wonder why we do not further analyze that matter to see if we might find some kind of solution to the problems of transportation services which are indebted and spend most of their revenues paying back interest.
I have with me a report for 1972. The net revenue of the CN amounted to $48,257,000; the interest to $66 million; the deficit is $17 million. Obviously, how could it be possible to improve a system with such a deficit due to interest on an almost priceless debt.
The St. Lawrence Seaway administration has a net revenue of $1,817,000; interests amounting to $22 million; and a deficit of $20,885,000.
Air Canada, which can definitely be termed an "in" service, had operation benefits of $45 million, a debt interest of $32 million; a net benefit of $8 million; and since 1963 the amount of interest paid is $199 million.
That is a very interesting side issue. Most members should spare the time to check and try to find some process, some form of payment, a type of loan which does not get them into endless debts, which they cannot ever

repay, all the transportation agencies and systems. That is why I felt it advisable to point out this situation at the beginning of my remarks.
However, when looking at the situation, it is easy to note, and I have explained the reasons first, that there are many contradictions in Canada's transportation system which is in a mess. That situation has been prevailing for quite some time, and there is nothing new to it. Federal governments, one after the other, recognized in principle that Canada needs a rational transportation system. By that, they mean a system through which the basic needs of the population in every part of Canada should be met by the most efficient and inexpensive means of transportation.
The MacPherson Royal Commission of inquiry was supposed to recommend the rationalization of the transportation services in Canada which compete each other and 'which are duplicated. The new Transport Act of 1967 wTas supposed to implement policies for the achievement of this aim. The new Canadian Transport Commission was supposed to have been empowered to implement that legislation. Unfortunately, it can be noted that the transportation situation has not improved sufficiently.
However, I must point out that the new Ottawa-Mont-real highway is greatly appreciated by drivers. All signs point to a reduction in the number of accidents. It is an improvement which is worth noticing. For the Ottawa-Montreal return trip, one can use a CN or CP train; one can also use the bus, or fly Air Canada. The yachtmen can even sail up the Ottawa river. However, it is not advisable to do so, as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) has already capsized, after hitting a submerged log. It is not a mode of transportation which can be recommended.
Which of these modes of transportation is the fastest, the most efficient and the cheapest? Undoubtedly, the train could be so, but the reduction of services and the increasing rates are going to make the train less attractive to potential travellers.
The more one examines the federal government's transportation policy, the more confused it seems. These various agencies compete each other, launch contradictory plans which have nothing in common except that they all cost millions to the taxpayers.
We have on the one hand the Canadian National, a Crown corporation, working at the systematic destruction of its passenger services with the wholehearted encouragement of the Canadian Transport Commission. Imagine, the federal regulatory body! But while the CTC lets railway companies get rid of their passenger trains, another government body, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is paying half the cost of a $2.5 million project to manufacture a high-speed passenger train.
During that period, the federal Department of Transport felt transportation services between Ottawa and Montreal were not sufficiently diversified. So they granted millions of dollars in subsidies to an undertaking named Air Industries Association of Canada in order to have another intercity transportation mode, called STOL-short take off and landing. Let us hope that service will prove satisfactory to the people, without reaching enormous costs.
March 7, 1975

It must be admitted that railway passenger service did not always get the kind of encouragement needed from all quarters, and this is due to a number of factors. It may be worthwhile to state a few. I shall mention schedules. They are frequently changed, without taking into account the needs of different regions.
The people in charge of Canadian National passenger services in particular, because I know them better than other services, should maintain more frequent consultations with train conductors to establish schedules one year ahead. Those employees, conductors and engineers, know the problems. Unfortunately they are not asked for their views. Consultation is a one-way proposition. Decisions are taken to stop here or stop there, but not elsewhere. Finally, people take the bus or other means of transportation.
I have here an article signed by Maurice Huot in the newspaper Montreal-Matin of November 29, 1974. It sums up the situation pretty neatly. Present circumstances warrant that the article be quoted in parts. It states:
The battle to revive railway passenger services was dealt a hard blow by former federal Liberal Minister of Transport J. W. Pickersgill.
According to a Canadian press dispatch from Ottawa, Mr. Pickersgill stated at a Carleton University seminar that if passenger trains disappear in Canada, in less than one year, no one in the country would be bored. In Mr. Pickersgill's opinion, the taxpayer should not be forced to pay for a few rich middle class passengers who use passenger trains between a few big cities. According to him, this money would be better spent if it were used to improve the freight service.
We are also reminded that the Transport Act passed in the House of Commons during the sixties created the transportation commission of which Mr. Pickersgill was the first chairman.
Indeed, Mr. Pickersgill had prepared a job for himself at a very interesting salary.
... It is under his administration that the commission allowed the railways to eliminate certain passenger train services while others were maintained with the help of federal grants. On the other hand, Mr. Jean Marchand blamed this act for the unfortunate situation of train transportation. For his part, Mr. Marchand wants to improve the passenger train services.
Of course, this issue is complex. It is certain that in Canada and the United States, train service is more popular with travellers. Should we not allow the travellers to have the choice of taking the train, the bus, or the plane for their business and pleasure trips?
In order to preserve oil energy, would it not be appropriate that more passengers take railway transit systems linking major cities? Is it not also by stimulating passenger railway transportation that the railway companies will make more profits from that means of transport and that the subsidies and grants will be decreasing?
Railway transportation is still very popular in Europe as well as in Asia for passengers, thanks to the improvement of tracks allowing higher speed. We do not quite understand why Mr. Pickersgill has intervened, given the present economic, technological and social situation.
In 1971, railway transport experts maintained that railways were not profitable in any country, except Switzerland. Recent statistics indicate that Japanese railways were operating in the red. And yet the railway service there was very good, as it was in France and Germany. Contrary to Canada those three countries decided once for all that railways had a social role to play in public transportation. This is what we must consider: a railway transit system, a genuine social service. We must provide the
Transportation
Canadian people with a passenger service because railways are quite safe and that they can run despite bad weather, when other means of transportation are paralyzed in certain circumstances.
We must think of the social role of a passenger service. Even though we will have to engage more public money, we know what has been the cost up to now. But if such a service could be improved we could then build up a good transportation service to accommodate all Canadian people, ensuring that in almost all occasions, except in a very few exceptions, public could enjoy a good service.
So I believe that Canadians would be satisfied with decisions of that sort and the railroads could be used with greater advantage than it is the case now.
The question is not whether the Canadian Pacific is more willing than the Canadian National or conversely, to attract business. The thing is to know when the government will finally say when it intends to provide transportation services more suited to the Canadian people.
Following the passage of the new 1967 Transport Act, the government is prepared to subsidize transport companies in respect of their losses, but one must stop and think that a subsidy is not a transportation policy. Other means must be sought. Recently, the disparities in freight rates caused great prejudice to a great many manufacturers, particularly those in my area, because I received representations to that effect.
Adjustments would have to be made because manufacturers in my area had to layoff people because freight costs were too high in various provinces, even if orders are waiting to be shipped. Once again, I hope the minister in co-operation with his colleagues can find a formula better suited to the needs of Canadians.
