speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak on transportation. This morning and early this afternoon I listened to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) give one of his great performances in the House. His hands were waving, and his delivery was faultless. But I remember hearing a similar speech before. He put up a wonderful show, and did it very well.
What he did reminded me of something I saw last Wednesday night. I was sitting in a movie theatre and just before the main feature came on they showed a cartoon which reminded me of the Minister of Transport. The cartoon was about a character known as the Roadrunner, who runs around at great speed, says "beep, beep," and

March 7, 1975
Transportation
really does not do much else, although what he does is very entertaining. He reminded me of the Minister of Transport. He is very entertaining, but he seldom says anything worthwhile.
What disturbed me about the minister's speech were his comments on racism. Madam Speaker, I have been here for three years and, to me, it always seems that allusions to racism come from the other side of the House. The people of Canada are tired of hearing them. I do not know what they have to do with transport policy in this country. Our criticism of the minister does not involve racism. We criticize him because he is incompetent, because his department does not know what it is doing, and because the people of Canada are fed up with the government's lack of policies in transportation.
At the beginning of his speech he took a shot at the Conservative party. He said it lacked policies and is lacking physically, intellectually, and morally. I wonder how the Minister of Transport could make a statement like that, after running around the country during the last federal election campaign and telling the people what his party would do for urban rapid transit, to make trains run and to build airports. So far we have not seen any legislation which would implement the policies the minister talked about in the last election campaign. I wonder how he can talk about a moral position.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUATE TRANSPORTATION POLICY-REQUEST THAT FUNCTION OF DEPARTMENT BE REVIEWED BY HOUSE
speechtext: Especially as the Liberal party is morally derelict.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUATE TRANSPORTATION POLICY-REQUEST THAT FUNCTION OF DEPARTMENT BE REVIEWED BY HOUSE
speechtext:
During the election campaign he spoke about an urban rapid transit policy. To my amazement, many of the things he said were taken right out of the policy pronouncement prepared by my party over one year before that. Some actual sentences were taken from my party's policy pronouncement. So, what is the minister thinking when he talks about my party's intellectual and moral qualities?
What is the government's attitude on the manufacture of aeroplanes in this country? The government paid de Havilland in Ontario, the builders of STOL aircraft, tens of millions of dollars in aid. Now the parent company, Hawker-Siddeley, wants the government to buy the de Havilland Aircraft because it does not think it will be successful.
Throughout the minister's 40 minute speech he kept asking for suggested solutions from my side of the House. Now he has left the House, just as we want to suggest solutions.
I draw the minister's attention to Dominion Aircraft Ltd., formerly of British Columbia. My party, and members of the minister's party were in favour of giving aid to that company to help it build STOL aircraft. The government refused. Now that company is in business in the state of Washington, south of British Columbia, employing people to build an aeroplane which should have been built in Canada.
Consider also what has happened to Trident Aircraft Ltd. of British Columbia, which has developed a float aircraft. The government gave the company $1.5 million as a PAIT grant. The individual owners of the company put up $1.5 million of their own capital. Now the government 
is telling these people that it will not put more money into the company, and the company may need to close down unless it is given assistance. These examples illustrate policies which people in my part of the country do not accept, and which the people of Canada will not accept.
I want to talk for a few minutes about airports in British Columbia. In 1966, the then minister of transport, J. W. Pickersgill, said:
The Department of Transport intends to acquire all of Sea Island eventually. The statement freezes the real estate market and subjects Sea Island to a de facto expropriation.
In 1973, only seven years later, there was still the same problem. All the homes have not yet been expropriated. The Hon. Jack Davis, then minister of the environment, said at that time:
No special environmental impact-study has been made on the effects of the airport expansion.
What kind of transport department comes up with these types of answers seven years after announcing an expansion of an airport, stating they have not yet come up with any environmental studies to let the residents know what will be the effects? The Hon. Jack Davis also said:
Expropriation on Sea Island is in line with Ottawa's decision years ago to clear the island of all private homes.
Since that time we have had government assurance that they do not want to go into all areas of Sea Island. We have asked for other studies of the area. We cannot get any answers. What kind of government comes forth with these kinds of policies?
The minister wants to talk about moral intellectual decisions of the Conservative party. I wish to read a letter sent by the Liberal party during the election campaign. It concerned the people of Sea Island. The letter was addressed "To the concerned Sea Island residents". Copies were delivered to people in the area and the media. I quote from it as follows:
The following is a statement released after several days of telephone negotiations with Ottawa and Mr. Ron Basford's office, through Liberal candidate Joan Wallace, Burnaby-Richmond-Delta:
Mr. Ron Basford has promised to sit down with Joan Wallace regardless if she wins her riding or not, to negotiate a fair and equitable settlement of the Sea Island expropriation and renters' problems. In addition, Mr. Basford will initiate the appointment of an impartial, new mediator to act on the discussed issues. Mr. Basford initiated this commitment on the premise that it will be accepted on an unbiased and objective level by the Sea Island group. The commitment was also made after repeated assurances by Joan Wallace's campaign manager that all parties involved in the preliminary discussion to date have been completely serious on ending this very serious problem and that the new mediating body would be respected in their judgment if empowered under the act.
No further clarification of what the new mediating body's form will be, i.e. one, two or three impartial people but the names as suggested during our meeting on Sea Island were put forward to Mr. Basford for
serious consideration.
It was pointed out that Mr. Isadore Wolfe will not be involved in the negotiations.
We believe that this is a major step forward and a very constructive one. Joan is very optimistic a compromise can be achieved very soon.
The preceding statement was negotiated through the office of Ron Green of the B.C. Liberal party headquarters.

Yours very truly,
for Joan Wallace, Campaign Office Sandy McLeod Campaign Manager
The people of Sea Island respected that statement made by the candidate in the last election and by the then Minister of State for Urban Affairs, now Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford). What happened after the election? The results were not as they wanted them. The people of Sea Island sent a telegram to Ottawa. They received back the following telegram:
Mr. W. Charles Johnstone, General Counsel, Sea Island Ratepayers Association.
I have your letter of July 11. No statement was enclosed but I presume you refer to a statement dated July 6 issued by Mr. Sandy McLeod. Mr. McLeod must be in error in that I have made none of the commitments alleged. Mr. Wolfe is special adviser to the government in this matter and your proper course is to deal with him.
The Honourable Ron Basford, Minister of State for Urban Affairs That was a complete reversal of what the government promised the residents of Sea Island. Nothing has been done to date. The residents of Sea Island are still there, waiting and wondering what is going to be done in their situation. There is a court decision. The residents finally had to take the government to the Federal Court of Canada to plead their case so they would not be kicked out of their homes. I will quote from the decision of that court so that we will know what the judge had to say after listening to both sides of the situation. I quote:
With reference to the Canadian Bill of Rights the learned counsel for respondents stressed that due process of law had not been followed in the present instance because the minister had not given proper assistance to seek and obtain alternative premises and had stopped negotiations as soon as actions were instituted for additional compensation.
In my opinion assistance has to be given if section 24(5) is to be meaningful, otherwise it is wholly optional to the minister to give or not give assistance. That subsection 5 of section 24 reads as follows:
(5) For the purposes of subparagraphs (3)(b)(ii) and (4)(b)(ii), consideration shall be given to the time and circumstances in which a former owner was allowed to continue in occupation of the land after the Crown became entitled to take physical possession or make use thereof, and to any assistance given by the minister to enable such former owner to seek and obtain alternative premises.
As per the evidence the assistance was not worthwhile.
That is a judge of the Federal Court saying that this minister and this government have not given proper assistance to the people of Sea Island. Until proper assistance is given, the problem will not be solved. I might mention that most Liberal members from British Columbia agree with the people of that area. They have met them and I think they have great sympathy for their problems.
The minister asked for solutions. I will give him a solution to the problem in that area. I want to talk about interest payments that have had to be made. They amount to over $700 a day. The government has paid over $250,000 in interest. That is money the government owes those people.
I want to compare the situation of the people of Sea Island with those in Pickering, Ontario. The original estimated cost in Pickering was $70 million. An additional 10 per cent payment made in August, 1973, increased the original market value across the board by $7 million. Agreement not to take possession until January, 1975, did
Transportation
not limit a final home for a home evaluation. That is a program which the people of Sea Island do not have.
In 1969, 88,000 acres were expropriated at Mirabel, Quebec. Of 3,180 owners, all but 112 were settled by March, 1973. However, in November, 1973, the government reopened claims and grants with a $16 million across the board adjustment. Why would they do that when only 112 claims were not settled out of a total of over 3,000? The government undertook arbitration of land values across the board on all claims, and revised the original estimate of cost per acre from $210 to $500.
In other areas of Canada where the government was considering building airports, it gave the people of those areas extra consideration. It has not given that consideration to the people of Sea Island. If it had given those people what they are asking for and what a judge of the Federal Court and a private appraiser says is reasonable, the problem would have been solved a long time ago. That is a solution for the minister. I hope he will consider it seriously and do something about it.
I do not have much time left. However, there are two other topics I want to mention. One is a motion which I presented to this House on April 16, 1973. It reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of transferring the Crown lands, commonly known as the Canadian Forces Station Ladner or the Old Boundary Bay Airport, together with buildings thereon, to the municipality of Delta and, in co-operation with the municipality, develop the areas as an industrial-recreational complex of pollution-free secondary industries, parkland, ocean beaches and sports stadia for the benefit of Delta, Richmond and the Lower Mainland and as an example to other medium-sized urban and suburban communities of the value of such a complex.
NDP and Liberal members spoke in favour of that motion. They thought it was a good idea. However, as of this date we do not have any report or study from the government. That was over two years ago. My latest letter from the minister's office is dated February 14. It states:
I will look into the matter you have raised and will be back in touch with you as soon as possible.
That motion was presented two years ago. If the government were serious, it would have solved the problem a long time ago. Studies in that area would have been completed and the people of that area would know what will be done with the land. It is just sitting there. It is vacant and an eyesore to the whole community.
When talking about transport and the awarding of a contract by the minister in the past few days to an American owned company, we raised some questions in the House. When talking about content, we still get conflicting answers. I say to the minister that content is the ownership of the company. If there is a Canadian company, it should have the advantage over an American company when a tender is being considered. Many members opposite agree. I hope the minister will reconsider his answer of this morning and look at the situation carefully. There are people in my area who are out of work because of the switch in the contract. All the profits will be going across the border. I do not see that as the proper way to have things happen.
I will complete my remarks on the subject of air routes. The minister spent a lot of time talking about CP Air and

Transportation
Air Canada and all the benefits of a government-owned airline over the the privately owned airline. As long as this minister is Minister of Transport, CP Air will continue to be at the low end of the scale. CP Air has suffered ever since this minister took over his portfolio.
The people of western Canada and Liberal members from British Columbia agree that CP Air should have been allowed the new routes into southern California. I know they had a meeting with the Minister of Transport to plead the case of CP Air with regard to those routes. It made a lot of sense for CP Air to have them rather than Air Canada. What did the minister do, Madam Speaker? He walked out. He would not even listen to his own members. If he is asking for positive suggestions, then I suggest he listen a little. The problem with the minister is that he does not listen. Not only does he not listen to the members on this side of the House; he does not listen to the members on his own side of the House.
Until I see a replacement sitting in the minister's seat in this House, I can see no solution to the major transportation problems. We need a minister on that side who is serious about the transportation problems of this country and who works full time on finding solutions to them. I should like to see one of the newer members on that side, perhaps one of the members from British Columbia, placed in the cabinet and put in charge of transportation. British Columbia only has one minister on that side, and that in itself is a slight on a province that elected eight Liberal members. In the last parliament there were four British Columbia Liberal members, and two of them were cabinet ministers. I am not including the member who went to the Senate. He was not elected by the people of British Columbia but was appointed to that place by the government.
I should like to see the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo) made minister of transport. She is a hard working woman, and it is International Women's Year. My final word is, "why not?" appoint the hon. member for Skeena minister of transport? Then perhaps we will be able to solve some of the transportation problems in this country.

Madam Speaker, I should like to congratulate the minister on his explanation to the House this afternoon of the difficulties that he has encountered in his department, on his sincerity in bringing these problems to the attention of the House some time ago, and on the positive steps he has taken to solve these problems.
At the same time one is left with the impression that his explanations to the House always seem to fall on deaf ears, or else the opposition turn their heads around and do not listen. Or they do as they did a few minutes ago, make catcalls, yelling across the House and not really listening to what the minister says to them. I am sure many of them even do not take the time to read Hansard the following day. That is obvious from the comments they have been making.

Another reason why it is obvious that they do not understand is that they continually make representations in the House on transportation matters, but repeat the same comments time after time. Each member of the opposition speaks as an individual on the problems of transportation in his own constituency. No real policies or concrete suggestions are put forward as to what they would do if they were in a position to do it. The role of the opposition is to put forward good, concrete criticism, not to indulge in personalities or to criticize individual members. It is constructive suggestions that will solve the transportation problems of this country.
I can assure hon. members opposite that the minister is not going to wait for them to make suggestions any longer, since they are all speaking as individuals. They do not come to grips with the problems. The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) spoke of the problems in his own constituency. Another member from the maritimes spoke of transportation problems in the maritimes, forgetting to tell the House, as the minister pointed out this afternoon, that in all phases of transportation, whether land, sea or air, the maritimes are subsidized to the tune of 50 per cent on all goods delivered. No member on the other side mentioned that because they are afraid it might hurt individual interests in their own areas.
What Canada needs is what the minister says it needs, a national transportation policy for the entire country.

Air Canada is not only the top notch international and domestic air carrier, but perhaps more important, it is an air carrier which has been, and continues to be, responsive to the needs of our people. Air Canada's safety record, which I would like to touch on, is unquestionably unparalleled by any other airline in the world.
The safety record of Air Canada is similar to the safety record of the CNR, which does have the best safety record of any railway in the world. It is often the case that members of the Conservative party, like the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie), seem to get some kind of sadistic satisfaction from continually accusing the airline in respect of its safety performance. What amazes me is the fact that people like that hon. member continue to paint the worst possible image of our country's flag carrier when he has not even taken the time to accept an invitation to inspect Air Canada's servicing facilities and to question on the spot the people responsible for servicing the aircraft.
I cannot and will not accept this as constructive criticism, and I certainly cannot accept it as a means of furthering our aviation interests around the world. If the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre finds, for some reason, that he must continue to decline invitations to visit and be briefed on Air Canada's maintenance facilities, then I suggest he should read the magazine called "Aircraft Engineering" of last November, which had a seven-page article about Air Canada under the heading "The Airline That Knows What Maintenance is All About".
Air Canada's transport air safety division is currently working on some 60 safety research projects. These range from wake turbulence from large jetliners to fire resistance of aircraft interiors. This has enabled the ministry to feed back to the aviation community the information derived from these studies, investigations and research. Such feedback has met with some strong favour from commercial and private pilots in Canada.
Air Canada has an inspiring flying record of safety, a record which matches our strict and stringent regulations. When it comes to air safety, this is one case where we put all our eggs in one basket. We are not scrimping on this one; we are not looking for ways to save a dollar here and a dollar there. Safety is expensive and it must be, because we want the very finest navigational aids, the best equipped airports and the best trained pilots. I am almost finished.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, keeping in mind his own statement that "transport is in a mess" in this country, I think it is time a number of specific questions were asked of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mar-chand). Answers to these questions will likely be few and far between if we are to judge by previous standards.
The whole realm of transportation could easily be said to need scrutiny, but I intend to limit my inquiries almost entirely to the problems of rail transportation. How the minister can allow a railway system which literally built this country to deteriorate in prestige, as it has, is beyond me. Even given the best of management, the government-owned railroad, the CN, cannot function without a clearly defined transportation policy. Railroads which are not government owned, such as CP and others, while not as reliant on this policy are also finding it extremely difficult to operate.
I have heard in the few years I have been here constant references to our transportation policy. Not yet, however, have I been presented with a single document which might possibly be construed as this proposed policy. Even a single step in the right direction might be cause for some hope. Just determining where to start may be, I suppose, a major problem. Another major problem I suggest might be whom to start with, as never have I encountered so many department heads, experts, chiefs, deputies, or whatever as were in attendance at the standing committee on transport yesterday. Even at the rate paid to MP's, and I am sure it easily exceeds that, it would cost well over $1,000 for the one hour that committee sat.
Some of my most serious questions to the minister over the past few years have concerned safety. Each year as the reports come to us from the Canadian Transport Commission the incidence of derailment increases. Going with this, hand in hand, are the frightening statistics in regard to deaths and injuries at level crossings of various kinds. Some of these are necessarily the result of outright carelessness on the part of pedestrians and motorists. What is of importance is the fact that a fully responsible transportation policy would eliminate all such crossings. Only in this way can we prepare for high-speed trains, such as the Turbo, that are surely essential in Canada. Realizing this, one would expect and hope that this simple portion of the policy might be presented. This and several other minor portions of policy would provide a glimmer of hope for things to come. How can we have any hope so long as these easy items are left unattended.
I have questioned the minister also on other types of accidents. Some of these involved fatalities and other serious injuries. To repeat all of them now would take far too much time. I only wish to make a few simple suggestions. Let us have some direction from the minister to the proper departments with regard to the basic standards acceptable in the maintenance of way. Let us have some direction from the minister with regard to safe levels of axle loadings on freight cars. Let us have some direction from the minister with regard to employee training and standards of conduct.
Only this one brief reference will I make to the report of the CTC of Tuesday last. Very seldom is a report such as
March 7, 1975

this issued as quickly as this one. Even when such speed is used I have never known of a report like this to be issued prior to a coroner's inquest. Yet in this case it was brought out exactly a week prior to the inquest. One of the most tragic accidents to occur recently is covered in this report. Until the inquest is completed I must necessarily hold my comments and I suggest the CTC might better have done likewise.
I feel that Canadian rail safety standards are years behind those in many other countries and, in my opinion, this situation has been created by a lack of initiative and direction on the part of the federal government. If this same government ever comes up with a reasonable way to ensure that the railways will run for a full year without interruption, that there are enough rail cars to deliver all of the grain and other products we have contracted for, we will surely need to have our safety standards improved to do the job properly.
In addition to the question of safety I would like to spend a few minutes on suggestions, or questions as you will, with regard to rail passenger lines. Again, in a country where a railway was the instrument of birth, we seem to have long since lost any initiative we may once have had. Canadian travellers have been plagued by increasing costs, an increasingly poor quality of service and, in general, are now substantially subsidizing a transportation system that operates contrary to the public interest.
It is common knowledge that the swift, safe movement of people in an economic manner is still best done by rail. Why then have we not high speed corridors, free of grade crossings between our major cities? Why are we continuing to use fossil fuels when the one source of energy Canada has in abundance, electricity, either hydro or nuclear generated, is so obviously a better choice? If the turbo has been proven, why are we not providing more of them for other runs? If not the turbo or perhaps the LRC, why are we not either developing our own technology or looking at foreign examples of high speed transit? With outmoded passenger facilities, poor service, poorer schedules is it any wonder that the lines are not profitable?
We are spending a huge sum of money on the STOL system from Ottawa to Montreal. As an experiment, I suppose I cannot argue, but as a long-term system there is no question in my mind that, given the same funds and backing, the railways could beat it every way-speed, service, economy, fuel savings, reliability. We have seen evidence in the United States of a resurgence of passenger rail traffic under its Amtrak system. That country, with all its industrial genius, is using the turbo and a turbopowered train imported from France, as well as conventional equipment. We do not need to set up a separate operating service. The CN is government-owned and, given proper direction and guidance, is completely capable of carrying out a government policy. Which, of course, brings me full circle.
In Canada we have the need, the desire, the technology, the ability, in fact all of the ingredients to be a leader in rail travel. What is needed, as I have said and I am sure my colleagues will repeat frequently, is a decent transportation policy. We do not have one now and will not have until we have a minister who is prepared to tackle the job
Transportation
properly. In any organization to do this you must start at the top and shake up the whole works. By the time you get to the area level such as Rideau area headquarters in Belleville you will soon find that these people, who are hard working and conscientious, will take their example from above.
My final question begs the obvious answer. Given the example we have seen in the House of Commons recently, is it any wonder that transportation is in a mess?

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity provided by the official opposition to discuss transportation as it refers to the maritimes in particular. Before proceeding further I should like to say why transportation is an issue of great concern to South Western Nova. My constituency is probably the greatest distance from Halifax and any other points in the maritimes on a time basis. This is one of the main reasons why we need a good transportation policy. It is absolutely necessary in the southern end of Nova Scotia to have ferries in order to reach our Canadian and United States markets by the most economic and fastest means available. I should like to mention the various industries pertaining to Nova Scotia at this end of the province.
In my constituency the fishing industry is probably the one element that is of prime concern to all of us. We have the highest value of fish landings of any area in Canada. This involves mainly lobster and other fresh fish. There is the problem of getting these products to the Canadian as well as the United States markets. Boats are required in this area. There are five particular ferries.
Before touching the subject of freight rates I wish to point out some of the areas in which the Ministry of Transport has been working in the last few years. I shall mention Digby, and point out that in 1971 a new Department of Transport wharf was built in order to facilitate the loading of boats with front and rear-end loading. Along with this the Department of Transport has maintained another wharf to facilitate the loading of freighters which carry pulpwood and more recently fish. This wharf not only brought a new boat to the area but in December, 1974, the Department of Transport bought the boat from the CPR, and since December 1974 the Princess of Acadia has been under the transport ministry.
I should add at this time that the people of the area are very happy with this take-over. For years they felt that there should be a more impressive service than that which they have had, a service that would be more in line with the cost of fares and in line with the other maritime ferry service. This is one area in which I believe the Ministry of Transport can play a vital role. The department has taken this lead already in respect of the purchase of the Princess of Acadia. I might also point out that the department maintains a wharf which is accessible to freighters which come in there.
Now I should like to turn to the Yarmouth area of my constituency. A new Ministry of Transport wharf has been under construction at Yarmouth since the beginning of this year, with an estimated value of $2.1 million. It is expected that this will be finished and in operation in the spring of 1976. This wharf will help carry the burden of

Transportation
handling the existing three ferries which come into the town of Yarmouth. One of the ferries is operated by the Canadian National under the Ministry of Transport. This ferry, called The Bluenose, is of great concern to the area. The Bluenose has been there for 17 years, and it is hoped that a larger boat might be available to handle the tourist traffic in the summer, and the truck traffic during the remainder of the year. Until now this service has not been quite adequate for the amount of traffic.
Now I would like to make a few comments about the tourist industry. The transportation policy at that end of the country brings a lot of tourists to the maritimes. This is probably the most convenient gateway from the United States, Ontario and Quebec to the maritimes.

I am sure that opposition members will recognize the fact that that is the policy of the federal government. The government, through the Minister of Transport, is working on such a policy and hopes to unveil it by late spring.
Now I would like to say something about federal-provincial consultations. We have a federal-provincial committee for Atlantic region transportation which the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) set up in 1969, shortly after introducing the Atlantic Region Freight

Assistance Act in the House. I would like to review some of the major recommendations that this committee made to the government, and the government's response to those recommendations.
One of the first major recommendations was for the introduction of a temporary trucking subsidy for intraregional traffic, to come into effect during the phasedown of the intraregional rail subsidy. The basic idea behind this proposal was to place the trucking industry on a competitive basis with the railways while the intraregional subsidy program was being phased out. This recommendation was accepted by the government and has been very effective in strengthening and building up the trucking industry in the Atlantic region.
More recently the federal and provincial governments have worked out a way of extending the westbound subsidy for rail and truck traffic to a level of 50 per cent on a selective basis. This was a first attempt at introducing selectivity into a direct subsidy program, and I think it is a tribute to our consultative mechanism that this was done with a high level of agreement between the government and the provinces concerned.
This program is beginning to show results, and we have seen examples of Atlantic region manufacturers who have attributed an increased penetration of central Canadian markets directly to this program.
I would like to quote from page 2 of the March 4 issue of the Halifax Chronicle-Herald. The headline of this article reads, "Transportation Costs 'Are Often Used as Whipping Boy' ". The article reads in part:
The effects of transportation costs on manufacturing industries in a region are "blown out of all proportions" on many occasions, Development Minister George Mitchell told the legislature last night...
The results of the study revealed it is "cheaper" to ship to practically any market in Canada from Sydney, than it is to ship from the Vilas plant outside Montreal, Mr. Mitchell said ...
Mr. Mitchell said such a situation exists due to the 50 per cent rail subsidy that has been successfully negotiated by the government, and "which clearly removed most arguments with respect to freight rates".
Then he points out the differences in prices and costs, and goes on to say that people who have a hasty, unresearched and negative manner sometimes do more harm than good to a province such as Nova Scotia.
Now I should like to return to some of the recommendations of the committee. The Department of Regional Economic Expansion, jointly with the four Atlantic provinces, established a physical distribution advisory service in Moncton designed to help the small shipper solve his total transportation problems, including such things as choice of mode, inventory control, warehousing, etc. So often in the past consultants have come to the area, done a good job, and taken their expertise away with them. We have in this organization the beginnings of a permanent source of expertise which will be of great value to local businessmen.
Again through this committee, a regional position was established on priorities for air services to and from and within the region. This was a significant input to the recent CTC inquiry on that subject.
In terms of total funding, the direct subsidy money paid under the Maritime Freight Rate Act and the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act has increased from $14.8

million in 1969 to $36 million in 1974. The full impact of the new selective westbound subsidy is not included in these figures, but it is expected to add a further $3 to $4 million in 1975.
Now I would like to direct the attention of hon. members to a meeting which was held in the Atlantic provinces in mid-January after the subsidy was dropped and freight rates went up all across Canada. This brought uniformity across Canada, and yet the maritimes retained their selective list of the 50 per cent subsidy on any product going west. At that time the Minister of Transport, in his statement in Halifax, mentioned that perhaps this might result in hardship in the area. However, he allowed for the fact that anyone suffering hardship could approach the provincial governments for assistance.
I hope that the effects of the lifting of the subsidy will start levelling out. Perhaps manufacturers in the maritimes will start filling the containers instead of sending them out half filled. Perhaps the advisory group in Moncton will assist them in this. Perhaps one should ask oneself where the money which previously went for the subsidy will now be directed. Perhaps the maritimes will put it into industry.
Having described to the House how the Department of Transport's policies have helped my constituency in the last few years and having spoken about the freight rate system, since I have some time left I would like to enumerate the major capital projects to which the department is committed. I will just read some of the highlights.
In Newfoundland the government plans to spend $19 million during the new fiscal year. The largest amount, $9.5 million, will be spent upgrading and developing terminals at Port-aux-Basques. The government will spend $2 million at the Goose Bay airport, nearly $1.5 million at the St. John's airport and $1 million toward a terminal at Cornerbrook. It will also spend $3.5 million toward the National Harbours Board terminal at St. John's.
In Nova Scotia the government will spend $8 million; $3.5 million of this will go toward adding facilities at the Halifax airport and another $2.3 million will go toward upgrading the terminal in North Sydney. This does not include, of course, the new wharf at Yarmouth.
In Prince Edward Island the government has earmarked half a million dollars toward the development of a new ferry terminal at Wood Islands. In New Brunswick it will spend $10.8 million during this fiscal year. The largest sum, $4.6 million, will go toward development of the Rodney terminal at Saint John, the estimated cost of which has been set at $37.5 million.
At Moncton the government will spend $2.5 million toward the construction of a new area control centre and related facilities to ensure air traffic safety. It will resurface and rebuild runways at Fredericton to the tune of $1.2 million, and in Saint John it will set up a harbour radar and collision avoidance system.
We are all aware of how important transportation is for the Atlantic region, placed as it is so far from its major markets. One might assume that if transportation had not been working well, there would have been a marked

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I want to touch briefly on some aspects of air and marine transport and some of the labour relations factors which in my opinion are hindering the viability of these important sectors of our transportation.
First I would like to suggest sincerely that there are many areas in transport that the government has been less than frank in disclosing to the public, and to hon. members of this House. There are many areas which need to be exposed by means of public inquiries, or at least referred to parliamentary committees, but so far the government appears to be more interested in covering up its own ineptitude than in corrective action.
I want to speak for a moment about Air Canada and the answer of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) to the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) on March 5, when the latter asked about the matter of Mr. Yves Menard's resignation from Air Canada. The Minister of Transport replied in the manner of the late Will Rogers that all he knew was what he read in the papers. He went on to say that the president of Air Canada was making an inquiry into the matter.
We in the opposition would like to know when the president of Air Canada and his capabilities will be the subject of an inquiry in this chamber, in view of the various difficulties facing this once efficient and respected airline.
Since we are speaking about Air Canada and the departure of one of its vice-presidents, I want to raise another matter, and I do so reluctantly, but I want to make it clear that I checked with Air Canada this morning in an attempt to get an answer. I have before me, and I will table it if requested to do so, a confidential interdepartmental letter to Mr. G. J. Kendall, assistant treasurer corporate finance. It is directed to this gentleman and is signed by the treasurer, Mr. H. N. Seath, and it states:
This is your authority to arrange for a cheque to be drawn as follows:
Date: March 11,1974.
Payee: P. J. Chartrand
Amount: $12,110.70.
The letter goes on to say:
This cheque should be charged to suspense and will be cleared by March 15,1974.
The cheque is to cover an advance on a second mortgage transferred from Mr. Chartrand to Morguard Trust Company. Authority for this transaction was provided by Mr. Pratte in his letter of March 14, 1973 to Mr. Chartrand.
This may be a perfectly innocent transaction. I do not know; it may be, but I would like to raise the question in

March 7, 1975
Transportation
this chamber of what justification there is for this sort of accommodation, if that is what it is, to a highly placed executive in our national airline. It may be perfectly innocent, but one has to ask whether this is, prima facie as we say in the legal profession, a good thing and something which would be available to the ordinary employee and, as far as that goes, to other employees in the operational or managerial levels of Air Canada? It is obvious that this type of financial service is not necessarily a good thing, and I would hope that this can be explained, and will be explained by the minister.
I suggest that our airline has become a refuge for many highly paid people who are not really necessary for its efficient operation. It has around 22,000 employees, twice as many, for example, as North West Orient Airlines of the United States, a company of comparable size. However, on the operations level where the work is done, Air Canada is often understaffed and its employees are asked to work longer hours than they would prefer. Its labour relations are abominable.
When the Canadian Airline Employees Association sought, for example, to take action a while ago against Air Canada because of a legitimate grievance, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) sat on CALEA's request pursuant to section 148 of Part V of the Canada Labour Code, for such a long time that the solicitor for CALEA was compelled on September 27, 1973, to write the following letter, part of which I quote:
The application for the minister's consent was filed on May 30th, 1973 and as you will recall, remained in the hands of the minister for a considerable period of time, a formal consent being received in this office on July 27th, 1973. It is perhaps more than coincidental that by the time the consent of the minister was received, the time prescribed by the Canada Labour Code for filing a complaint with the Board had expired.
The attitude of Air Canada from a labour relations point of view is terrible. So is the record. A partial list of labour disputes Air Canada has had in the past couple of years would indicate, briefly, that, in 1968 there was a work to rule; in 1969 there was a strike; in 1971 there were rotating strikes by the International Association of Machinists; in 1971 the CALEA people had a work to rule; in 1973 there was an 81 day strike in the finance division in Winnipeg; in 1973 there were rotating strikes by IAM again; in 1974 there were rotating strikes again by CALEA; in 1974 another wildcat by the IAM.
Also there have been continuing problems with CALPA and CALFA which have not resulted in strikes yet, and I emphasize yet. The situation at the finance branch at Winnipeg, as hon. members on the government side know, is chaotic, to put it mildly. There is approximately 100 man years of labour backlog of work required to clean up the situation, and in the meantime the computer capability of Air Canada is very badly fouled up, to say the least.
I have here a comparative balance sheet of assets and liabilities, another so-called confidential document which will be tabled in due course later, I presume, and there is some very interesting data on this as well. For example, looking at it we wonder why the accounts receivable have gone up from $102,278,000 in 1973 to $127,290,000 in the comparable period in 1974. There may be a perfectly logical explanation for this, but it is $25 million difference. The bank loan, on the other hand, was shown as $26

million in 1973. There is no trace of it in 1974, leading one to assume that it must have been put into the long term funding, which has gone up by over $200 million.
The unearned transportation revenue has gone up from $27,280,000 to $44,402,000. All this is going to make very fertile questioning areas in committee if we ever get these people into committee, and if it is possible that a proper audit can ever take place of Air Canada's operations.
The situation is so bad that it almost defies belief as far as the finance situation is concerned. I have interdepartmental correspondence here which indicates, for example, that there is an account which usually has a balance of $25,000 to $50,000. This is an account usually used in dealings with other airlines and what they call an OAL account. Yet in correspondence between Mr. J. C. Looney, manager of the interline accounting in Winnipeg and Mr. R. F. Kirby, manager of passenger accounting, dated late last year, the following excerpt appears:
This account normally has a balance of $25,000 to $50,000.
However, the letter goes on to say:
Therefore, the average balance in this account in the latter part of 1973 rose by about $10 million and at year end was some $14 million higher than normal.
During 1974, the account balance dropped significantly because OAL exchanges on hand but unprocessed were not accrued until the November 1974 month end.
The letter goes on to say:
This backlog has resulted in significant delays in billing other airlines. The balance in this account was in excess of $19 million in October, 1973 and as at November 30, 1974 was $10 million.
This is the part that is shocking where the letter says:
The cost of late billing is estimated in excess of $1 million using a 10 per cent interest rate ...
That is $1 million that is directly attributable to the deficit that this airline has incurred simply because it was not capable of collecting its accounts receivable. If that would not be cause for the resignation of the people responsible for the situation in the management of Air Canada, I do not know what would, Mr. Speaker. Surely the Minister of Transport must exercise more guidance over the various components of this department than he has done to date.
Anyone who has followed the progress of the SIU-and I am going to speak about the SIU here because it is related to marine transport and is a very important union-as it supposedly valiantly seeks to reform itself, must be disappointed at how long this is taking, particularly in view of the revelations on the front page of the Toronto Sun and other newspapers today. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) recognized that there may have been difficulties affecting the rights of union members from abuses perpetrated by their own union, but it seems to me he was slow to do anything about it.
The attempt by Mr. Gralewicz, president of the SIU, to sabotage a speech given last night by a former vice president, Mr. Lazarus, indicates that perhaps he is not the finest example of a sympathetic enlightened union leader, particularly when one considers the material that is available to document this. It would by superfluous to put on
March 7, 1975

the record at this time the many newspaper stories detailing particulars of the abuses within the SIU, yet members have to sit here every day and listen to platitudes. One such platitude was advanced by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacGuigan) on December 19 in reply to a matter I had raised. He quoted from the final report of the trustees who had to take over the operations of the SIU a decade ago, as follows:
The undemocratic union practices of the past no longer prevail and the individual rights of seamen are sufficiently well protected both in law and in practice.
What rubbish, Madam Speaker, when well known underworld figures are associated with the SIU, when a former vice president calls for a probe of the organization of the SIU charging beatings, and rigged votes, when the province of Ontario has made a similar request, when private investigators are hired by the union and presumably paid for by union dues to shadow dissident members. It is interesting to know that the price is not right because the SIU recently raised its dues, presumably to pay for the extra overhead. How much longer are the Minister of Transport and the government going to procrastinate before they call for an inquiry into this whole matter?
There is something else I should like to touch on briefly and about which the minister and I have had some dialogue already, that is, the Desjardins report. Madam Speaker, I deplore-and this is only my own submission which I do not suggest has any special weight-the way the terms of reference for Mr. Desjardins were set out. As I have already stated they required, among other things, that the investigation should not be subject to the customary rules of evidence nor evidence taken under oath, and that the investigation should not be conducted by means of public hearings.
I indicated to the minister that I would make some comments about the report itself and there are a few things that I should like to bring to his attention which, if they are true, certainly shock me. Although this report is dated July 30, 1974, the submissions of the Laurentian Pilotage Authority made to Mr. Desjardins do not necessarily follow through on this particular date.
The submissions of the LPA through Mr. Guy Major, were dated August 1, 1974, and supplemented on August 15, 1974, as indicated on page 2 of the report. That is to say these submissions appear to have been made after the report was written.
The submissions of the St. Lawrence River Pilots Association were made on July 30, 1974, and supplemented on August 2, 1974, according to page 3 of the report. Again, it appears submissions were made afterwards. Notwithstanding any observations about the propriety of this course of action, the submissions in support are well out of the time set out in the Pilotage Act, section 14(4), namely 30 days following publication in the Canada Gazette. I would point out that publication in the Canada Gazette took place on May 18, 1974.
These observations are rather disturbing, at least to me, and I hope the Minister of Tranport will consider them in due course because they seem to indicate that the report is not as bona fide as it should be. It is strange that it follows almost immediately upon an identical report under the
Transportation
same terms of reference made by Mr. Marler which came to an opposite conclusion.
One of the big difficulties about Crown corporations which come under the Minister of Transport is that they are reluctant to supply the type of information that is readily available from private corporations. I was told by a very reliable person who was participating in labour negotiations with PWA that they, PWA, are more frank in disclosing certain information than is Air Canada. The anti-labour bias of Air Canada is well known to anyone who has more than a fleeting knowledge of what goes on in it.
What this country needs, is for the government to have enough integrity to look into the obvious sloppy practices, complacency and carelessness that has permeated a great deal of its operations.
It is time that the people running this country made a commitment to honesty, and changed their priorities from doing anything to remain in power to justifying their continuing in office.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUATE TRANSPORTATION POLICY-REQUEST THAT FUNCTION OF DEPARTMENT BE REVIEWED BY HOUSE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I understand that a number of members still wish to speak so I shall co-operate by taking less than half the time that is allotted to me. I rise in this debate on the operations of the Department of Transport to register once again my complaint that the department is so slow in doing something effective about the pensions of retired railway workers, especially Canadian National and Canadian Pacific.
I recognize that in recent negotiations between employees and management the question of the terms and conditions of the various railway pension plans has been put on the bargaining table. But the discussions that take place in collective bargaining regarding railway pensions relate only to pension arrangements in the future for those now working. There is no way in which the plight of those already retired gets to the bargaining table when negotiations take place between railway employees and railway management. In my view that is where the government has to step in, Madam Speaker.
I do not think it is good enough for the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), or others in the cabinet, to mouth repeatedly the proposition that the Canadian National must be left to run its own show and that we do not own the Canadian Pacific Railway. These are both public institutions and are responsible to the people of Canada. I think the federal government has an obligation to say this to both these major railways, and to others like the Northern Alberta Railway and the Ontario Northland. The people of Canada want all of their retired railway workers to be given a better deal.
I recognize also that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) some months ago appointed Dr. Noel Hall as a commissioner to go into all aspects of railway pensions. I therefore have reason to believe that when Dr. Hall makes his report he will have something to say about railway pension plans so far as they affect those still working, and also that he will have something to say about the plight of those who are now retired. But somehow or other reports

March 7, 1975
Transportation
of commissions seem to take some time to come forward and I do not think it is appropriate for the government, Canadian National or Canadian Pacific, to stall just because Dr. Hall has not made his report.
Let me say in particular that, after much effort over many years, we were able to convince Canadian National that it should escalate the pensions of those already retired by 2 per cent each year. Last year, in 1974, Canadian National did better and escalated pensions by 4 per cent. But that escalation was still far below the actual rise in the cost of living. So far, in 1975, Canadian National has not escalated its pensions at all. I do not accept the excuse that the Hall report has not come forward. Whatever the Hall report will say will deal merely with matters of detail.
I think Canadian National should now be providing a 1975 escalation in the pensions of those already retired. That escalation should be in the order of at least 10 per cent, which was the increase given to retired public servants, retired members of the RCMP, retired armed forces personnel, and so on. That, also, represents roughly the amount of increase in the old age security pension, the guaranteed income supplement, war disability pensions, war veterans allowances, and so on.
The fact that many of these pensions and allowances which come under the aegis of the government have been increased makes one point clear. The government, having recognized the need to escalate pensions after retirement in those other areas mentioned, should carry that thinking through and say to both railway companies that they must do it, too.
I look forward to the publication eventually of the Hall report. I hope it will be a good one; I dare to believe that it will be. But I submit that action should be taken now to increase immediately the pensions of railway workers already retired.
I shall say another sentence or two, and then sit down. Another issue which must be dealt with in terms of railway pensions is the percentage of the pension paid to the widow. The idea that if the husband lives on, his wife having first died, he can get the full 100 per cent pension, but that if he dies his widow must get by on a 50 per cent pension belongs to a bygone age, to an age which existed before International Women's Year.

It may be too much to hope that the rate will go up to 100 per cent very soon, but, at least, it ought to be increased to 60 per cent or 75 per cent right now. I have time for one more brief sentence. I agreed to keep my remarks brief. I plead with the Minister of Transport to act on the important issue of getting an increase in the pensions of railway workers already retired, and that he do so right away.

Some hon. members opposite, I believe, were on the committee which dealt with that. They also include the question of rate groupings, the highway strengthening program signed by the four western provinces since the conference, the western northland highway program, which involves highways going to northern Canada and across the western provinces. The Committee also dealt with the problem of British Columbia ferries, the problem of the development of the port of Churchill-

Transportation
The committee that arose as a result of the WEOC conference is dealing with a formula for examining those branch lines in western Canada. This formula is acceptable to the four provincial governments involved. That is certainly progress when it comes to dealing with that particular area.
The establishment of a mechanism of consultation between the federal government and the four western provinces is one of the key developments of the WEOC conference of a year or two ago.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUATE TRANSPORTATION POLICY-REQUEST THAT FUNCTION OF DEPARTMENT BE REVIEWED BY HOUSE
speechtext: What are they complaining about?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUATE TRANSPORTATION POLICY-REQUEST THAT FUNCTION OF DEPARTMENT BE REVIEWED BY HOUSE
speechtext:
They are not complaining. You are not hearing complaints from the four western premiers and their ministers insofar as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) and transportation policies are concerned. They are sitting down and talking about the issues rather than standing up and haranguing, as members opposite have been doing for many months. Communiques from the western premiers and press statements from them are available to members opposite. They certainly have enthusiastic praise for the Minister of Transport and for his sincere effort to deal with the problems of transportation in western Canada.
I can quote some figures. Members opposite are not paying attention. Obviously they do not want to hear the facts. The northwest rail program in British Columbia involves an expenditure of well over $100 million. The Ashcroft Clinton has already been referred to; there was also the development of the port of Prince Rupert, various terminals on the west coast and a number of other things which could be mentioned to illustrate the fact that progress is being made, even though many members opposite missed that fact.
With regard to the question of air policy, there has been a very definite provincial input into domestic air operations. There have been discussions with the governments of Manitoba and Saskatchewan with regard to development of a third level air carrier and third level air service. That information is in the hands of the two western provinces. The federal government has made that information available to those two provinces. I am sure that before very long there will be an air service in operation as a result of federal initiative and assistance.
I referred to the fact that we now have cost disclosure of confidential cost data from the railroads. This was made available to the provincial governments for the first time last year so they can seek to determine the rightness or wrongness of freight rates for various commodities in their provinces. That came about entirely as a result of the WEOC conference in Calgary. Legislation introduced earlier this session confirms that that process is there today. It was not there for 100 years.
Just the other day the Minister of Transport forwarded to the western transport ministers copies of CN and CPR quick cost formulae to enable those in the provincial offices to look at railway costing procedures on various commodities that come to their attention. That is the first time this type of data has ever been released, let alone to the provincial governments. I say again, it is about time

March 7, 1975
Transportation
this was done. It is now forthcoming. Information is available to the provinces to enable them to assess better the kinds of policies and programs the various regions in Canada want to see the federal government bring forward.
The provincial officials have met with the CTC a number of times to discuss the more technical aspects of analysing this cost data. There has been a great deal of progress in that respect. By the same token, the western provinces, and I am sure this will also hold true for other provinces, are now providing the federal government with confidential information on trucking cost data and other material which up until this time has been almost completely within the provincial field. This is the kind of co-operation we have now. This progress has been as a result of the WEOC conference and the federal-provincial committee set up following it.
The entire consultative progress is a very essential first step if we are going to develop a rapport with the provinces, the agencies involved, the shippers, the suppliers and the people using the service. If we are going to develop policies for the various regions of Canada we must have this honest and open exchange of information and, Mr. Speaker, we are getting that.
The third major area of progress since WEOC is in the formulation of studies. I will be the first to admit that progress on some of these studies has been a little slow. However, the mere fact that some of them are being undertaken jointly with the provinces indicates ample progress. Some of these studies will be undertaken before very long. They will deal, for example, with new methods of setting freights rates for western Canada. If they prove worthwhile, they will apply to other areas of Canada. The pricing impact study, rail roadbed cost study and joint track usage study have been talked about for a long time without their feasibility having been determined one way or another.
I wish to refer to the 22 anomalies which were raised not too many days ago in the transport committee. The entire list of 22 anomalies was presented to the federal government. They have been rectified in the sense that they have been categorized. The different kinds of anomalies have been sorted out. These anomalies will be analysed and dealt with. If necessary, there will be legislative changes.
In conclusion I wish to quote from a press clipping that appeared in the February 26 edition of the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix. The headline is "Lougheed lauds transport pact". Premier Lougheed is known to many members opposite. I quote:
The accord reached Monday at a meeting of federal and provincial transportation ministers in Calgary was a major breakthrough for western Canada, Premier Peter Lougheed said-
That is what one western government, well known to members opposite, thinks of the progress in transportation policy that has been made by this minister and this government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the tirade, abuse and nonsense that came from the other side of the House this afternoon are enough to make a member wonder what in God's name he is doing in Ottawa on this Friday afternoon. I might be home if the airplanes were flying.

I wonder what happened to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand). He left the chamber about an hour ago. I am told he went to the hole downstairs to categorize over the French television network the debate this afternoon as a racial attack against him because he happens to be from the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUATE TRANSPORTATION POLICY-REQUEST THAT FUNCTION OF DEPARTMENT BE REVIEWED BY HOUSE
speechtext: Who said that?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUATE TRANSPORTATION POLICY-REQUEST THAT FUNCTION OF DEPARTMENT BE REVIEWED BY HOUSE
speechtext:
The minister himself. The minister said to offer some solutions. I will suggest some things that should be done immediately, and they will be welcomed by all Canadians.
# (1650)
The government can get on with ratifying the UNCTAD agreement with respect to the new code of ethics for Atlantic conferences, and retain for Canada the $1.5 billion we have already poured into them. All it takes is a signature on a piece of paper.
With regard to equal opportunities between the ports and the National Harbours Board, because the port of Montreal is dying we have a shed rental policy about to be imposed on eastern ports. For what purpose, Mr. Speaker? To remove the difference between the cost of doing business in the port of Halifax and the cost of doing business in the port of Montreal, so that hopefully traffic will be diverted from Halifax and Saint John to Montreal. I say it will not be diverted. Let the government take a corrective step. It will not be diverted to Montreal; this traffic will go to the port of New York. Is that what hon. members opposite want?
We want a firm commitment to identify and charge some department, some departmental group or agency, with responsibility for maritime policy. The statement made a few weeks ago by the minister is not good enough.
I refer to the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Sauve). She set up a committee on oceanology policy,4 and the other day we learned that it has not met for six months. Let us set up that committee and get on with it; again all it needs is a stroke of the pen. Let us strike the committee and get on with the steps required to establish a national maritime fleet. Let us announce our position on UNCTAD.
Do hon. members opposite want to know something else they can do with the stroke of a pen? They can bring into the House one sentence in a piece of legislation that will close the Atlantic, the Pacific and Arctic waters north of 60 degrees for passage solely by Canadian ships, with Canadian crews and flying Canadian flags. Save our extractive industries in the north. Do not let Murray River iron ore go into Europe in foreign bottoms; let us save it for Canadian bottoms.
The government can fire Yves Pratte, present chairman of the board of Air Canada, with the stroke of a pen.
We could ask the hon. member for South Western Nova (Miss Campbell) not to be so selective in her quotations. I notice that today she did not bother to quote Professor Wilson of the University of New Brunswick regarding subsidies on maritime freight rates. Do not let us hear too much more unmitigated nonsense about being subsidized in the maritimes on the movement of goods. Of course we are. We have to be. Look where we are.

We are talking about a total program costing $126 million over the last eight years. Last year it cost over $300 million just to pick up the interest and deficit on the operation of the St. Lawrence seaway, so hon. members opposite need not cry to us about how the maritimes are being subsidized. I ask them to make a simple decision. National transportation in Canada requires the will of the government to recognize that it must be subsidized if it is to serve the people adequately from one end of the country to the other. Let hon. members opposite not accuse us of not putting forward constructive suggestions because we have been doing that for the last ten or 12 years.
The other day we had an announcement from the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) concerning shipbuilding subsidies, a program we welcomed and which we urge he continued. We are not opposed to it in any way, shape or form. The Export Development Corporation does an extraordinarily good job of enabling Canadian yards to attract offshore business. The other day the minister did not bother to come to the House but gave his report to a few selected reporters, and it was circulated the following day. In that report he removed the word "temporary" and said the program would be permanent, and his flacks at $1,900 a speech patted themselves on their backs and said "What a wonderful job we have done".
If hon. members look at the report very closely they will find another story. The subsidy is to be reduced by one per cent a year until it is down from 14 per cent to 8 per cent; or rather from 17 per cent if you get a matching grant for modernization, reconstruction and upgrading of shipyards. Instead of giving the shipyards notice so there would not be an unnecessary and undue interruption in long-term planning for renewal and modernization, the minister, who believes we are spending too much on them already, starts the reduction next year right in the middle of programming and budgeting for shipyards. Why did he not say that in two years' time, or three years' time-whatever the necessary period is to accommodate present planning-he will start reducing the subsidy by one per cent? He did not do that.
In addition, the minister extended the subsidy to federal shipping, ships built for the federal government, which incidentally must now have the third largest navy in the world, though we still have not got any cargo bottoms to generate new dollars or to save some of the $1.5 billion we are throwing away offshore.
Business of the House
I should like to pose a question to the parliamentary secretary. In the announcement of the extension of the subsidization program to ships built for federal agencies and departments, why did he not announce that it was also being extended to ships built for provincial governments and agencies? Why did he leave out the provinces? I hope it was an oversight, and if it was then with a stroke of the pen he can make a minor amendment, or issue another press release, and correct the situation.
I have referred to five or six areas, Mr. Speaker, but I think the response from the other side of the chamber to the sincere and meaningful points that have been put forward by members from one end of the country to the other is both deplorable and regrettable. The absence of the minister in the last hour of the debate is also deplorable and regrettable. Even the parliamentary secretary for DREE, who still thinks he is the be all and end all in transportation, I notice has left the chamber.
We have welcomed the opportunity this afternoon to draw attention to a number of points regarding the shortcomings in transportation services and the tremendous difficulties being faced by the transportation community in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED INADEQUATE TRANSPORTATION POLICY-REQUEST THAT FUNCTION OF DEPARTMENT BE REVIEWED BY HOUSE
speechtext: Order, please. It being five o'clock p.m. it is my duty to inform the House that, pursuant to section (11) of Standing Order 58, the proceedings on the motion have expired.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether I might ask the government House leader if he is in a position to tell us what we will be considering on Tuesday and Wednesday.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when I was asked this question yesterday I said I hoped I would have some consultations with the House leaders on Monday and agree on what might be a mutually satisfactory program.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
It being five o'clock p.m. this House stands adjourned until Monday next at two o'clock p.m., pursuant to Standing Order 2(1).
